data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The night-time UHI gap is primarily an evapotranspiration deficit: impervious urban surfaces shed water and suppress latent heat loss, leaving more net radiation to heat the air; the gap scales with the scarcity of urban vegetation and irrigation.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If a city is heavily irrigated or has extensive green space, latent heat loss may match rural rates and shrink the UHI gap.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If rural soil moisture is very low (e.g., desert), the rural latent heat flux is also negligible and the gap is driven by other factors.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If anthropogenic heat or cloud cover dominates the nocturnal energy balance, the evapotranspiration deficit is not the primary mechanism.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"In the countryside, evapotranspiration converts incoming and stored energy to latent heat, cooling the near-surface air; cities, being drier and impervious, cannot shed heat this way after sunset, so the sensible heat flux remains higher, and the gap is more pronounced in arid or less vegetated cities.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
